The tone system of Kara is not treated at all in previous studies; in the present study, we provide only the brief description of tone. Thus, the detailed and comprehensive analysis of the tone pattern of Kara is left open for other scholars for further investigation. Kara is a register tone language with two tones labeled as high and low. ... In a similar way, tone makes lexical distinction in Kara as exemplified by examples in (101) below. new_statements.quote: Kara, like other Omotic languages, exhibits contrastive tone. The tone system of Kara is not treated at all in previous studies; in the present study, we provide only the brief description of tone. [...] Kara is a register tone language with two tones labeled as high and low. [...] In a similar way, tone makes lexical distinction in Kara as exemplified by examples in (101) below. The tone bearing units are vowels. [p. 63] [...] In disyllabic words, all possible combination of tone pattern is attested, but in monosyllabic words either H or L tone is observed. [p. 63] [...] Our data show that the grammatical function of tone is insignificant. [...] As a matter of fact, tone is largely left unmarked in the present study. [p. 64]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kara is described as a two-tone (H/L) register tone language with lexical tone on vowels (minimal pairs like gòbà 'to run' vs góbá 'respect'); every H/L combination occurs in disyllables. The grammar says nothing whatsoever about word stress or accent — no stress rule, no statement that stress is absent, no prominence marking in the wordlist (the apostrophe in forms like bakˈala marks ejectives). The only prosodic statement is the tone description; the author calls the tone analysis 'shallow' and leaves it for further study.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the author notes tone is only superficially described, that its grammatical function appears 'insignificant' (except imperative suffixes -ma/-mate 'pronounced with high tone', p. 174), and that tone is largely left unmarked in the rest of the thesis
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone on isolated nouns and verbs (infinitive as citation form); no phrase-level or stress domain discussed
new_statements.identity_note: Alemgena Belete 2018 describes the Kara (= Karo, kxh, Glottolog karo1297) of the three Omo-bank villages Dus, Korcho (Qorcho) and Labuk, data chiefly from Dus Kebele; it treats Kara as a distinct South Omotic language (citing Moges Yigezu 2007 for the vowel system and lexical comparison with Hamar). Ethnologue/Wikipedia sometimes list Kara as a dialect of Hamer-Banna (hame1242); the catalog entry for hame1242 (Petrollino 2016, stress) does NOT cover Kara — Petrollino states her Kara exposure was limited to one text and some vocabulary (p. 6).

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/suprasegmental: no hits). Sec. 2.4 Tone pp. 63-64: Kara is a register tone language with two tones H and L, lexically contrastive, TBU = vowel; tone analysis explicitly called brief/shallow and left for future work.

Bibliographic only: descriptive refs are Alemgena 2018 (grammar) and Epple 2010 (Bashada ethnography listed as grammar sketch); alternate names Kara, Kerre, Cherre, Hamar-Koke; Tsuge 1996 subclassification comment.
